ami_style_notes: The meeting shifts from informal, rapid exchanges of short turns to long, structured presentations, then back to medium-length question-and-answer turns. Overlap is light but frequent backchannels (“yeah,” “right,” “okay”) and occasional cut-ins give it a live, conversational feel. Speakers use fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections, especially when asking questions or explaining an idea aloud. Their tone is friendly and collegial even when the presentations become more formal. Questions often begin with praise or a softener, then unfold through clarification and follow-ups; uncertainty is expressed with phrases such as “I think,” “maybe,” and “I’m not sure.” Participants build on one another’s points, while challenges tend to be indirect and framed as curiosity rather than disagreement.
research_problem: How schools should compare the benefits of outdoor learning programs for student learning and participation

speakers.name: Marisol Vega
speakers.background: A district-partnered education researcher with 11 years of experience studying elementary inquiry instruction. She has conducted classroom ethnography, teacher interviews, and analyses of student work, and coordinates school access and observation schedules for this study.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats participation as situated in classroom relationships and instructional routines. In garden and park activities, she looks for contributions such as careful observation, building on a peer's idea, and recording findings—not just speaking frequency. She wants teacher knowledge to inform how observers interpret quieter students' actions, but is unsure how to preserve that context in a comparison across the two programs.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Daniel Okafor
speakers.background: A developmental psychologist with nine years of experience studying peer collaboration and attention in middle childhood. He has designed time-sampling observation protocols, trained coders, and assessed inter-rater agreement in school-based studies; he manages observer training and data quality for this study.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He approaches participation as behavior that must be defined clearly enough for different observers to identify it in both settings. He worries that garden and park lessons offer different opportunities to speak, move, and handle materials, which could make an apparent program difference a measurement artifact. He favors a feasible shared observation protocol but is willing to revise its categories if they miss meaningful, less visible contributions.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

benchmark_task: Identify one unstated premise connecting a discipline's measurement method to a shared research decision about a broader outcome. Cite the actual dialogue for the method, goal, and decision; do not assume the premise is false.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Identify one unstated premise connecting a discipline's measurement method to a shared research decision about a broader outcome. Cite the actual dialogue for the method, goal, and decision; do not assume the premise is false.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Have the developmental psychologist propose coding student-initiated task contributions during standardized 15-minute small-group observation windows. Have the team discuss its broader goal of comparing how the garden and local-park programs benefit student learning and participation, then jointly select that coding measure as the primary participation outcome for the next comparison. Let the distinction between observable contributions and other forms of participation create natural friction with the education researcher. The conversation should leave unstated the premise that students have sufficiently comparable opportunities to make codable contributions in the two programs. Participants should not label or explicitly flag that premise. Include enough dialogue about the method, goal, and decision for an evaluator to cite the actual transcript; do not prewrite turns or quotations.

ground_truth.assumption: Students have sufficiently comparable opportunities to make student-initiated, codable task contributions during the observation windows in both programs for the counts to serve as a comparable indicator of participation.
ground_truth.dependent_decision: Use the developmental psychologist's observation coding as the primary participation outcome in the next-stage garden-versus-local-park comparison.
ground_truth.disciplinary_context: Developmental psychology supplies the behavioral observation method; education research raises the question of whether that method captures participation as schools understand it. The shared research goal is to compare the programs' benefits for student learning and participation.
ground_truth.why_needed: The joint decision treats differences in coded contribution counts as informative about participation across programs. That interpretation depends on students having comparable chances to produce the behavior being counted.
ground_truth.risk_if_false: If opportunities to make codable contributions differ substantially between the programs, the primary measure could attribute a difference in activity structure to a difference in student participation.

transcript.text: Yeah, I did. The notes have a few kids contributing by pointing something out or starting a group record without saying much, so a speech-only count would miss them. I’m thinking a 15-minute small-group window in each setting, coding student-initiated task contributions—verbal or observable nonverbal ones. transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, the 15-minute window feels workable. transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, let’s try that. I’d drop “student-initiated” from the outcome if taking up a peer’s idea counts; we can code that separately from introducing a new observation. transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, that boundary makes sense. transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, I’ll pull an ambiguous garden case and an ambiguous park case, and note what the teacher debriefs add to each. transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor

qa_feedback.inference: The team chooses contribution counts as a primary outcome for comparing participation across settings. Interpreting differences in those counts as participation differences depends on comparable opportunities to contribute. Daniel explicitly raises that concern in turn 10 by proposing to check whether one lesson gives children more openings than the other.
